report.releaseDate: 12 Nov 2026 (Caixa Econômica Federal 3T26 financial statements / Relatório da Administração; trade-press pick-up 13–17 Nov 2026)
report.currency: BRL (R$) — tables in R$ millions unless stated; USD equivalents in parentheses at ~5.78 BRL/USD
report.verdict: A record but visibly decelerating nine months: federal lottery sales of R$18.71bn (~$3.24bn), +3.9% YoY, with Q3 up only +1.3% to R$6.51bn (~$1.13bn) as the July-2025 average ticket repricing (+21.7%) lapped — nominal growth is now below any plausible inflation print, the operating-cost ratio rose 240bps to 21.1% of sales, and the retail network shrank again. Social transfers of R$7.10bn (~$1.23bn, +3.4%) and a 48% public take of R$8.97bn (~$1.55bn) are the structural positives; the parent quietly dropped lotteries from its headline results package this quarter, which tells you how management reads the trend.
summary: **Entity and listing status clarified.** CAIXA Loterias S.A. is an unlisted, closed-capital (capital fechado) sociedade anônima and a wholly-owned subsidiary of Caixa Econômica Federal (itself 100% federally owned); it has no traded equity, so there is no share-price reaction, EPS or consensus to benchmark against. Fiscal year is the calendar year (3T26 = Jul–Sep 2026); 9M = Jan–Sep 2026. Caixa's 3T25 management report describes its object as operating lotteries, bets, games and similar services under the federal concession.

**Headline: record 9M sales, but the slowest quarter of the year.** Lottery sales (arrecadação) reached R$18,706m (~$3,236m) in 9M-26, +3.9% YoY vs R$17,998m (~$3,114m); Q3-26 was R$6,514m (~$1,127m), +1.3% YoY vs R$6,429m (~$1,112m) and +4.6% QoQ vs R$6,225m (~$1,077m). All four outlets we read (Gaming Intelligence, BNLData, Sigma World, Focus Gaming News) relay the same figures from Caixa's 3T26 Relatório da Administração, and Q1+Q2+Q3 (5,967+6,225+6,514) reconciles to the 9M total within rounding.

**Growth has decelerated every quarter: +8.4% (Q1) → +2.6% (Q2) → +1.3% (Q3).** The pattern maps exactly onto the July-2025 repricing, when the 12 games took an average ticket-price increase of 21.7%. Q1/Q2-26 were still comparing against pre-hike quarters; Q3-26 is the first clean comparison and shows that underlying growth ex-price is roughly nil in nominal terms. BNLData explicitly notes the variations are nominal and not inflation-adjusted — in real terms Q3 volumes are contracting.

**Price, not volume, carried 2026.** With sales up +8.4% in Q1 against a +21.7% price lift, implied bet volumes fell double-digit in H1; the Q3 +1.3% print therefore reflects a lower-volume, higher-ticket base. Mega-Sena rollover sequences (two consecutive draws in late Feb/early Mar alone generated ~R$247.6m, ~$43m) flattered Q1 — jackpot luck, not structural demand, is the swing factor each quarter.

**Statutory public take rose ~100bps to ~48% of sales.** Transfers to legal beneficiaries were R$7,096m (~$1,228m) in 9M-26 (+3.4%; 37.9% of sales) and R$2,481m (~$429m) in Q3 (+1.6% YoY, +5.0% QoQ). Add income tax withheld on prizes of R$1,874m (~$324m, +17.4%) and the federal lotteries directed R$8,970m (~$1,552m) to taxes and public purposes in 9M-26 — c.48.0% of sales vs an estimated 47.0% a year earlier, with the delta entirely from prize tax.

**Where the Q3 money went.** Social security (Seguridade Social) R$1,100m (~$190m, ~44% of transfers), public security (FNSP) R$628m (~$109m), sport R$471m (~$81m, −0.8% YoY), culture R$185m (~$32m), education R$92m (~$16m). For 9M, sport received R$1,361m (~$235m, +4.9%) — the line Caixa chose to highlight — while education fell 11.0% to R$260m (~$45m) from R$292m (~$51m), the largest decline of any beneficiary.

**Prizes: 9M R$6,331m (~$1,095m), +4.0%, a stable 33.8% of sales.** In Q3 the net prize line fell 5.7% QoQ and 3.3% YoY; Caixa cautions the figure follows payment date and can include prior-quarter bets, so the quarterly move is timing noise rather than a payout-ratio change.

**Cost creep is the lowlight management is not talking about.** Custeio e manutenção — which Caixa says includes the Lottery Development Fund (FDL) and remuneration of the lotérica retail network — rose 22.8% QoQ and 14.2% YoY in Q3, lifting its share of sales from 18.7% to 21.1% (we estimate ~R$1,374m, ~$238m, vs ~R$1,202m, ~$208m, in 3T25). On a +1.3% sales print, a +14% cost line compresses whatever residual accrues to Caixa/the subsidiary.

**Distribution footprint keeps contracting.** Lotéricas numbered 12,917 at end-September, −21 QoQ and −137 YoY (−1.0%); non-betting banking transactions through the network fell 9.8% YoY to 387m in Q3. The lottery business depends on this channel's economics; a shrinking, less-trafficked network is a structural headwind unless digital mix (not disclosed in the material we could access) is filling the gap.

**Management is burying the line.** BNLData notes that, unlike 3T25 when lotteries were a highlighted result, Caixa's 3T26 press release, results presentation and performance-analysis report make no mention of them; the data appear only in the Relatório da Administração. The parent's own recurring net income was R$3,486m (~$603m), −7.4% YoY and −10.6% QoQ, with NPLs at 4.01% — attention is elsewhere.

**No guidance, no cost-transformation programme, no capital-return framework.** Neither Caixa Loterias nor Caixa issues lottery sales guidance; no restructuring or efficiency programme with amounts/target years is disclosed; as a wholly-owned statutory operator there are no buybacks or dividends to third parties. The only 'programme' is the July-2025 repricing, whose stated aims (3T25 report) were higher sales/social transfers and product sustainability — the volume response says the elasticity was higher than hoped.

**The 'cannibalisation' thesis is not supported by Caixa's own numbers.** With the regulated online betting market in full operation since Jan-2025, federal lottery sales hit a record R$26.61bn (~$4.60bn) in FY25 (vs R$25.91bn, ~$4.48bn, in 2024 and R$23.4bn, ~$4.05bn, in 2023) and are +3.9% in 9M-26, while federal bets tax receipts reached R$11.12bn (~$1.92bn) in Jan–Sep 2026, already 11.7% above all of 2025. That said, real-terms lottery stagnation post-repricing leaves room for both narratives.

**Regulatory overhang is political, not statutory.** BNLData reports a bill criminalising bets is blocking the Chamber of Deputies' agenda amid government pressure, with Caixa joining the public commentary. A rollback of regulated betting would be a relative positive for the lottery monopoly; the more immediate uncertainty is Caixa's own stated intent (President Carlos Vieira, earlier in 2026) to enter sports betting/online gaming with a ~R$7bn (~$1.2bn) 2026 ambition — status [unverified] in the material we could access.

**Q1 seasonality framed the year.** Q1-26 sales of R$5,967m (~$1,032m) were −30.7% vs Q4-25 (implied R$8,612m, ~$1,490m), underscoring how Mega da Virada makes Q4 the swing quarter; FY26 will be decided by the December jackpot cycle, not by Q3.

**Product concentration remains extreme.** Mega-Sena (~40%) and Lotofácil (~35%) accounted for 74.8% of Q1-26 sales (72.2% in 3T25, when the pair grew +25.3% on the price hike); no 9M-26 product split was available in the sources we could read. Two games with rollover-driven volatility define the P&L.

**Responsible-gaming credentials maintained.** Caixa Loterias holds WLA Responsible Gaming Level 3 certification and submitted its recertification application during Q3-26 — relevant for any future digital/betting expansion under the federal framework.

**Disclosure gap: the subsidiary's own P&L is not in the public narrative.** Caixa Loterias publishes quarterly financial statements (e.g. 30-Jun-2025 DFs) but its 3T26 revenue, net income, cash and debt could not be verified here; the arrecadação figures are gross consumer stakes, not the subsidiary's revenue. Readers should treat 'sales' as GGR-equivalent volume, not operator revenue.

**Thesis read-through.** For sector investors this is a clean data point on (i) lottery price elasticity in an emerging market — a +21.7% price move bought roughly one year of nominal growth and is now behind the business; (ii) the absence of measurable cannibalisation from regulated bets at the aggregate level; and (iii) rising statutory/channel cost share, which matters for anyone modelling a future Caixa betting entry or a Lotex/instant-lottery relaunch on the same retail backbone.

segments.name: Federal lotteries — sales & product mix (sole operating segment)
segments.headline: Record 9M of R$18.71bn (~$3.24bn), +3.9%, but Q3 +1.3% as the July-2025 price hike laps; underlying volume is flat-to-down in nominal terms and negative in real terms.
narrative: They booked R$6,514m (~$1,127m) of lottery stakes in Q3-26, 4.6% above Q2's R$6,225m (~$1,077m) and 1.3% above the R$6,429m (~$1,112m) of 3T25, taking the nine-month total to R$18,706m (~$3,236m) against R$17,998m (~$3,114m) a year earlier. On the face of it that is a third consecutive record nine months, extending the FY25 record of R$26.61bn (~$4.60bn) which itself followed R$25.91bn (~$4.48bn) in 2024 and R$23.4bn (~$4.05bn) in 2023. The composition of the growth is the problem. The 12 games took an average ticket-price increase of 21.7% in July 2025, so Q1-26 (+8.4% to R$5,967m, ~$1,032m) and Q2-26 (+2.6%) were still comparing against unrepriced quarters; Q3-26 is the first clean comparison and it shows growth of just 1.3% nominal — a decline in real terms at any plausible IPCA print — and BNLData is careful to note that none of these variations is inflation-adjusted. Arithmetically, a +21.7% price lift against +8.4% and +2.6% sales growth in H1 implies underlying bet volumes down well into double digits; the Q3 print simply confirms that the base has reset lower.

The mix remains dominated by two games. Mega-Sena (~40% of stakes) and Lotofácil (~35%) accounted for 74.8% of Q1-26 sales, up from 72.2% in 3T25 when the pair grew a combined 25.3% on the back of the repricing, while the long tail — Quina, Lotomania, Dupla Sena, Timemania, Dia de Sorte, Super Sete, +Milionária, Loteca and the passive Loteria Federal — splits the remaining quarter; Dupla Sena and Timemania together were cited at R$620.7m (~$107m) in the 3T25 report (period basis unclear). Caixa attributed the 'positive' Q1 result to a sequence of accumulated draws, with concursos 2978 and 2979 alone taking R$123.6m and R$124m (~R$247.6m, ~$43m); no product split for Q3 or 9M-26 was available in the sources we could read, and the absence of that disclosure in a quarter where sport transfers (which are keyed to specific games) fell 0.8% YoY suggests the tail games, not the two flagships, are where volume is leaking.

Luck and seasonality dominate the quarterly cadence. Q1-26 was 30.7% below Q4-25 (implied R$8,612m, ~$1,490m, from FY25 less 9M25), because the Mega da Virada year-end draw makes Q4 the structural peak; Q3's +4.6% sequential gain is the normal winter uplift plus rollover timing rather than evidence of re-acceleration. We would characterise the run-rate as: price-driven growth exhausted, volume soft, jackpot cycles providing ±3–5 percentage points of quarterly noise. There is no disclosure of actives, ARPU, online penetration or marketing spend in any of the materials we could access, so customer-economics analysis of the kind available for listed peers is not possible — a disclosure gap worth noting for any future Caixa betting vehicle that might reference this franchise.

Management offered no segment guidance, and the tone of the parent's 3T26 package is telling: having showcased lotteries in the 3T25 release, Caixa dropped them entirely from the 3T26 press release, results presentation and performance-analysis report, leaving the numbers only in the Relatório da Administração. The stated objectives of the 2025 repricing — raising stakes and social transfers while protecting product 'sustainability, continuity and attractiveness' — have been met on the first two counts in nominal terms and arguably failed on the third. Our judgement is that FY26 sales land at roughly R$27.3–27.6bn (~$4.72–4.77bn, +2.6% to +3.7%, estimate), with Q4 entirely dependent on the December jackpot cycle; a weak Mega da Virada and a further step-down in the tail games would push FY growth below 2%.

segments.name: Statutory proceeds waterfall — social transfers, prize tax and operating cost
segments.headline: Public take ~48% of 9M sales (R$8.97bn, ~$1.55bn), up ~100bps on prize tax; custeio & manutenção jumped to 21.1% of Q3 sales (+240bps), the quarter's real negative.
narrative: They transferred R$2,481m (~$429m) to the legal beneficiaries in Q3-26, 5.0% more than Q2 and 1.6% more than 3T25, bringing the nine-month total to R$7,096m (~$1,228m), +3.4% YoY. The transfer ratio is essentially fixed by statute — 38.1% of stakes in Q3 and 37.9% for 9M, within 20bps of the prior-year ratios — so this line will always track sales; the 3.4% growth lagging the 3.9% sales growth reflects nothing more than quarterly rounding and the prize-payment timing that feeds the base. Within Q3, social security took R$1,100m (~$190m, ~44% of transfers), the public-security fund R$628m (~$109m), sport R$471m (~$81m), culture R$185m (~$32m) and education R$92m (~$16m). For the nine months Caixa chose to highlight sport, which received R$1,361m (~$235m), +4.9%; it did not highlight that sport's Q3 allocation fell 0.8% YoY, nor that education — the smallest beneficiary — saw the year's largest decline, −11.0% to R$260m (~$45m) from R$292m (~$51m).

The fiscal line grew far faster than the social one. Income tax withheld on prizes reached R$1,874m (~$324m) in 9M-26, +17.4%, of which R$504m (~$87m) fell in Q3; because the H1 figure was R$1,370m (~$237m, +31.8%), we estimate 3T25 prize tax at ~R$557m (~$96m) and therefore a ~9.5% YoY decline in Q3 — consistent with the −3.3% drop in net prizes paid and with Caixa's caveat that prizes are booked on payment date and may include prior-quarter bets. Combining transfers and prize tax, the federal lotteries directed R$8,970m (~$1,552m) to taxes and public purposes in 9M-26 — 48.0% of stakes against an estimated 47.0% (R$8,459m, ~$1,463m) a year earlier — with the whole ~100bps increase coming from the tax line rather than any change in the beneficiary split. Note that Focus Gaming News quotes 'R$10bn to social programmes (+45.7%)' for 9M-26; this is irreconcilable with the R$7,096m carried by BNLData and Sigma World and with Focus's own R$6.86bn 9M25 base (which equals the BNLData-implied prior-year transfer figure), so we use the lower number.

The line that deserves attention is custeio e manutenção, which Caixa defines as including the Lottery Development Fund (FDL) and remuneration of the lotérica network. It rose 22.8% QoQ and 14.2% YoY in Q3, lifting its share of stakes from 18.7% to 21.1% — on our arithmetic roughly R$1,374m (~$238m) versus ~R$1,202m (~$208m) in 3T25 and ~R$1,119m (~$194m, ~18.0% of sales) in Q2-26. No explanation was offered. The candidates are a step-up in retailer commission rates or incentive payments to stabilise a shrinking network, higher FDL contributions tied to product or systems investment, or a reclassification; whichever it is, a cost line growing 14% against sales growing 1% is incompatible with a stable operator margin, and it lands before any revenue from the parent's mooted betting entry. Net prizes of R$6,331m (~$1,095m) in 9M were a stable 33.8% of stakes, so the prize ratio is not the offset.

Stacking the disclosed lines for 9M — prizes 33.8%, transfers 37.9%, prize tax 10.0% — leaves a residual of roughly R$3.4bn (~$0.59bn, ~18.2% of stakes, estimate) to cover custeio, FDL and whatever accrues to Caixa Loterias and its parent, versus ~19.2% a year earlier; given the Q3 custeio ratio of 21.1% the exit-rate residual is thinner still. This is the closest thing to an 'EBITDA margin' trend available for an operator that discloses no P&L in the material we could read, and it is moving the wrong way. There is no cost-transformation programme, no stated target ratio and no guidance; the only visible management action is a recertification application to the WLA (Responsible Gaming Level 3), submitted in Q3, which has no economic bearing.

segments.name: Distribution network — lotéricas, channels and responsible gaming
segments.headline: 12,917 lotéricas at Sep-26 (−137 YoY, −21 QoQ) and non-betting footfall −9.8%: the physical backbone is eroding while channel-cost share rises.
narrative: They ended September with 12,917 lottery retail units, 21 fewer than in June and 137 fewer than a year earlier (−1.0% YoY, from 13,054). The network is the exclusive physical point of sale for the federal games and also a bank-correspondent channel for Caixa; non-betting banking transactions through the lotéricas fell 9.8% YoY to 387m in Q3, which matters because the agents' economics rest on both revenue streams. Stakes per lotérica (annualised Q3, estimate) were ~R$2.02m (~$349k), up ~2.4% YoY — i.e. network shrinkage slightly outpaced sales growth, so productivity per door improved only because doors closed, not because demand rose.

Read alongside the custeio line, the channel picture is one of rising cost to hold a shrinking footprint: remuneration of the lotéricas sits inside the custeio e manutenção bucket that rose 14.2% YoY against a 1.3% sales increase. Whether Caixa raised commission rates to arrest attrition, or whether FDL spending on terminals/systems drove the increase, is not disclosed; either way the operator is paying more per real of stakes. The digital channel (Loterias Online / the Loterias CAIXA app) is the obvious mitigant, but no online share, actives or app metrics appeared in any source we could access, so we cannot say whether digital is substituting for the lost physical capacity or merely cannibalising it. For comparison, listed lottery operators in Europe typically report online shares of 30–50% of draw-based sales; the absence of that datapoint here is itself informative.

The electoral calendar introduced a small Q4 disturbance: the presidential second round on 25 October 2026 altered the draw schedule for the federal games, which will shift a handful of concursos between weeks but should not move the quarter materially. Caixa Loterias holds WLA Responsible Gaming Level 3 certification and completed submission of its recertification request during Q3; this is table stakes for a state lottery and would be a prerequisite for any Caixa-branded online betting or instant-win expansion.

Our view is that the network is a slow-burn structural negative that the repricing has temporarily masked. With real-terms stakes now declining, the bank's non-betting footfall through the channel falling at a high-single-digit rate, and no disclosed digital offset, the risk is a feedback loop in which weaker agent economics drive further closures that then weigh on stakes — the scenario in which the custeio ratio keeps rising. Watch the lotérica count in the FY26 report and any disclosure of online share; a figure above ~15–20% would change our read.

blocks.takeaway: The network is a slow-burn structural negative that repricing temporarily masked, risking a feedback loop of closures and rising custeio.

Weaker agent economics could drive closures that weigh on stakes, keeping the custeio ratio rising.
Watch the lotérica count in the FY26 report and any online-share disclosure; a figure above ~15–20% would change our read.

highlights.text: Record 9M stakes of R$18,706m (~$3,236m), +3.9% YoY, and a third straight record nine months — delivered with Brazil's regulated online betting market fully operational, undermining the cannibalisation thesis at the aggregate level.

Statutory public take rose to ~48.0% of stakes: R$8,970m (~$1,552m) to transfers and prize tax in 9M-26, with transfers to legal beneficiaries R$7,096m (~$1,228m, +3.4%) and sport funding R$1,361m (~$235m, +4.9%).
Income tax withheld on prizes R$1,874m (~$324m) in 9M, +17.4% — a jackpot-cycle windfall for the Treasury that will not repeat mechanically (Q3 alone was ~−9.5% YoY on our estimate).
Q3 sequential recovery of +4.6% QoQ to R$6,514m (~$1,127m) and a stable 33.8% prize ratio show the price-adjusted base has found a floor; no payout deterioration.

Productivity per door edged up ~2.4% YoY to ~R$2.02m (~$349k) annualised stakes per lotérica, and WLA Responsible Gaming Level 3 recertification was submitted — credentials intact for any digital/betting extension.
The July-2025 repricing (+21.7% average ticket) is now fully in the base, so from Q4-26 the comparison is clean; any Mega da Virada upside flows straight through to YoY growth.

lowlights.text: Growth decelerated every quarter — +8.4% (Q1) → +2.6% (Q2) → +1.3% (Q3) — as the +21.7% price lift lapped; nominal growth is below inflation and implied bet volumes fell double-digit in H1. Price bought one year of growth, not a new trajectory.

Custeio & manutenção (FDL + lotérica remuneration) +14.2% YoY and +22.8% QoQ in Q3, lifting the ratio 240bps to 21.1% of stakes (~R$1,374m, ~$238m est.) against +1.3% sales growth — unexplained, and the single most important margin datapoint in the release.
Retail backbone shrinking: 12,917 lotéricas (−137 YoY, −21 QoQ) and non-betting banking transactions −9.8% YoY to 387m, with no disclosed online share to show digital is filling the gap.

Management de-emphasis and disclosure retreat: lotteries were dropped from Caixa's 3T26 press release, presentation and performance report (featured in 3T25); no Q3/9M product mix, no operator P&L, no actives/ARPU, no guidance.

Education transfers −11.0% to R$260m (~$45m) in 9M and sport −0.8% YoY in Q3 — the tail games that feed specific beneficiaries appear to be where volume is leaking, even as flagship Mega-Sena/Lotofácil concentration rises above 74%.

Political/regulatory noise: a bill criminalising bets is blocking the Chamber agenda, Caixa has joined the cannibalisation commentary, and the parent's own ~R$7bn (~$1.2bn) 2026 betting ambition remains unverified — strategic direction of the franchise is unclear while the parent's recurring net income fell 7.4% YoY to R$3,486m (~$603m).

Secondary-source discrepancy: Focus Gaming News' 'R$10bn (+45.7%) to social programmes' for 9M-26 conflicts with the R$7,096m (+3.4%) carried by BNLData/Sigma; we could not open the primary PDF to adjudicate and have used the lower figure.

forecast.intro: There is no guidance to bridge: neither CAIXA Loterias S.A. nor Caixa Econômica Federal issues lottery sales, transfer or margin targets, and no cost or efficiency programme with amounts or target years is disclosed. The only quantified management action is the July-2025 average ticket repricing of +21.7% across the 12 games, whose stated aims were higher stakes/social transfers and product sustainability. The 'bridge' below is therefore our own reconstruction from the FY25 base through the 9M-26 actual to an FY26 estimate, with Q4 — the Mega da Virada quarter — the only moving part that matters. The sole operating segment (federal draw-based lotteries) drives everything; the deceleration is a price-lapping effect concentrated in the tail games, with Mega-Sena/Lotofácil rollover luck as the quarterly swing.

bridge.title: Q4-26E (Mega da Virada quarter) — analyst estimate

forecast.view: **Revenue/volume:** we model Q4-26 stakes of R$8.6–8.9bn (~$1.49–1.54bn), i.e. 0–3% above the implied Q4-25 base of R$8,612m, giving FY26 of R$27.3–27.6bn (~$4.72–4.77bn), +2.6% to +3.7% — a clean price-free comparison for the first time since mid-2025, with the outcome hinging on the Mega da Virada prize pool and whether a rollover sequence lands in December. Our central case (+1.5% Q4, FY26 ≈ R$27.4bn, ~$4.74bn) assumes volumes stay flat in real terms; a weak jackpot cycle pushes FY growth below 2% and would make 2026 the first real-terms decline since the 2025 Q1 trough (−10%). **Margin/cost:** the key unknown is whether the Q3 custeio ratio of 21.1% is a step-change (commission or FDL reset) or a timing spike; we assume partial normalisation to ~19.5–20% in Q4 but flag that a sustained 21% ratio removes ~R$150–200m (~$26–35m) per quarter from the operator residual versus the 18.7% of 3T25. Prize ratio ~33.8% and transfer ratio ~38% are statutory and will not move. **Leverage/capital:** not applicable — no third-party debt or capital-return framework identified; the subsidiary is funded within the Caixa group [unverified]. **Swing factors:** (i) December jackpot luck; (ii) any further ticket repricing, which we would now view as volume-destructive; (iii) the bets-criminalisation bill — a ban would be a relative positive for the lottery monopoly but signals policy instability; (iv) a formal launch of Caixa's own betting product, which would re-rate the strategic value of the lotérica/app distribution but also compete for the same wallet; (v) lotérica attrition accelerating beyond ~1%/yr. **Net:** modest nominal growth, flat-to-negative real growth, rising channel cost — a mature cash franchise for the Treasury, not a growth story.
watch: Mega da Virada 2026 estimated prize pool and whether a Mega-Sena rollover sequence lands in Q4 (Q4-25 implied base R$8,612m, ~$1,490m)
Custeio & manutenção ratio in Q4/FY26: does it revert toward 18.7% or hold at ~21%? Any explanation of lotérica commission or FDL changes
Lotérica count at Dec-26 (12,917 at Sep-26; −1.0% YoY) and any first disclosure of online/app share of stakes

Progress of the bets-criminalisation bill in the Chamber and the government's use of the lottery-cannibalisation argument; Caixa's own online betting launch status (~R$7bn, ~$1.2bn 2026 ambition stated earlier in 2026)
Publication of Caixa Loterias S.A.'s own 3T26/FY26 financial statements (service revenue, net income, cash) to put an operator P&L behind the stakes figures
9M/FY26 product split: is tail-game (Quina, Lotomania, Dupla Sena, Timemania, Loteca) volume loss accelerating beyond the Mega-Sena/Lotofácil flagships (74.8% of Q1-26)?
Any further ticket repricing proposals — given the volume response to the July-2025 +21.7% move, a second round would be a red flag
WLA Responsible Gaming Level 3 recertification outcome and any instant-lottery (Lotex-type) or digital product announcements

report.confidenceNote: MEDIUM on the headline stakes figures (Q3-26 R$6,514m; 9M-26 R$18,706m; +1.3%/+3.9%): four independent outlets (Gaming Intelligence, BNLData, Sigma World, Focus Gaming News) relay the same numbers from Caixa's 3T26 Relatório da Administração, and Q1+Q2+Q3 reconciles to 9M within rounding. LOW on the sub-lines (net prizes, custeio & manutenção, lotérica count, banking transactions, beneficiary split): these rest mainly on BNLData with partial Focus Gaming News corroboration. IMPORTANT: the primary filings (Caixa Loterias S.A. Relatório da Administração/DFs 3T26 and Caixa Econômica Federal's 3T26 Relatório da Administração) could not be opened — the fetch tool returned access errors and the session's web-tool quota was then exhausted — so no figure in this note was read directly from the filing. Not verified / not available: Caixa Loterias' own revenue, net income, cash and debt; 9M-26 product mix; online channel share; actives/ARPU; the status of Caixa's betting entry; Brazilian inflation for the real-terms comparison. Items marked 'est.' are our arithmetic (e.g. 3T25 prize tax ~R$557m derived from the 9M and H1 growth rates; custeio R$ amounts derived from the disclosed % of sales; Q4-25 implied from FY25 less 9M25). Discrepancy flagged: Focus Gaming News' 'R$10bn (+45.7%) to social programmes 9M-26' vs BNLData/Sigma R$7,096m (+3.4%) — we use the latter. FX: USD/BRL ~5.78 implied from the contemporaneous conversions published by Focus Gaming News and Sigma World on 12–17 Nov 2026 (not an independently retrieved central-bank fix); EUR/BRL ~6.22 implied by Gaming Intelligence (R$18.71bn = €3.01bn). All USD figures are approximate and prefixed '~'.
report.sharePriceReaction: Not applicable — CAIXA Loterias S.A. is an unlisted, closed-capital wholly-owned subsidiary of Caixa Econômica Federal, which is itself 100% owned by the Federal Union; no traded equity or bonds of the subsidiary were identified. The listed sister company Caixa Seguridade (B3: CXSE3, insurance) does not consolidate the lottery line and is unaffected.
